etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English miserie, from Old French miserie (modern: misère), from Latin miseria, from miser, equivalent to miser +‎ -y. Doublet of misère.

definitions.definition: Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; distress; woe.

quote.citation: 1578–1579, Edmund Spenser, “Prosopopoia. Or Mother Hubberds Tale. [...] Dedicated to the Right Honorable the Ladie Compton and Mountegle”, in Complaints. Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie. Whereof the Next Page Maketh Mention‎[1], London: Imprinted for VVilliam Ponsonbie, dwelling in Paules Churchyard at the signe of the Bishops head, published 1591, →OCLC:
quote.text: For miſerie doth braueſt mindes abate, / And make them ſeeke for that they wont to ſcorne, / Of fortune and of hope at once forlorne.

quote.citation: 2008, Charlotte Bingham, The Land of Summer‎[2]:
quote.text: It was not just the confusion that unhappiness brings, it was not just the loneliness, it was the despair that accompanies all those emotions that turns unhappiness into utter misery.

quote.citation: 2022 January 12, Nigel Harris, “Comment: Unhappy start to 2022”, in RAIL, number 948, page 3:
quote.text: Then, in January, a creeping tsunami of train cancellations, triggered by major staff absences as a result of the aggressive transmissibility of Omicron, heaped further misery on rail users.

definitions.definition: (US and UK, dialects) A bodily ache or pain.

quote.citation: 1868, John Vestal Hadley, Seven Months a Prisoner, page 15:
quote.text: [...] and I had a misery in my left breast and shoulder. I was hurt, but knew not how or how much.

quote.citation: 1593, anonymous author, The Life and Death of Iacke Straw […], Act I:
quote.text: The Widdow that hath but a pan of braſſe,  […] Muſt pay her Landlord many a groat,Or twil be puld out of her throat:  […] The rich haue all, the poore liue in miſerie:  […]
